title: Write a Kafka consumer that routes failed messages to a dead-letter queue.
shortTitle: Write a Kafka consumer that routes failed messages to a dead-letter queue.

s1_definition.oneliner: A DLQ consumer tries to process, retries transient failures, and on a poison message publishes the original plus failure details to a dead-letter topic and commits, so one bad record never blocks or is lost.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)** -- a separate topic where a consumer sends messages it cannot process after exhausting retries, so a single bad message does not block or get dropped.
- **Poison pill** -- a record that always fails, like malformed data or a business rule it can never satisfy; the DLQ pattern moves it aside safely.
- **Retry classification** -- transient failures (timeouts, network) are retried with backoff; permanent failures (deserialization, validation) go straight to the DLQ.
- **Failure metadata** -- the DLQ record preserves the original key and value and adds headers with the exception, original topic, partition, offset, and timestamp.
- **Commit ordering** -- commit the source offset only after the record is either processed successfully or confirmed written to the DLQ.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a settlement clerk at National Bank of India who hits a transfer slip that is torn and unreadable. If the clerk keeps retrying forever, the whole tray stalls. Instead, after a couple of attempts, the clerk places the bad slip in a clearly labelled problem tray with a note explaining what went wrong, then moves on. Nothing is lost and nothing is blocked, and a supervisor can later examine the problem tray.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A dead-letter queue is a separate topic where a consumer sends messages it cannot process, so a single poison message never blocks the partition and is never silently dropped. I classify failures as transient or permanent, retry transient ones with backoff, and route permanent ones or exhausted retries to the DLQ with full failure metadata.

The critical ordering is that I commit the source offset only after the record is either processed successfully or confirmed written to the DLQ. If the DLQ write fails, I do not commit, so the record is retried rather than lost.

In my National Bank of India settlement service, occasional malformed transfers used to block the partition. We added a DLQ with failure headers, classified errors, and committed only after each record was handled. We also alerted on DLQ depth and built a redrive job for fixed messages.

Remember one sentence: a DLQ consumer routes poison messages aside with failure metadata so the partition advances without losing data, and commits only after process or DLQ-write succeeds.

---

keyPoints: A dead-letter queue moves poison messages aside so a single bad record never blocks the partition.
Classify failures: transient ones are retried with backoff, permanent ones go straight to the DLQ.
Preserve original key, value, and add headers with exception details, original offset, and retry count.
Commit the source offset only after the record is processed successfully or confirmed written to the DLQ.
If the DLQ write itself fails, do not commit so the record is retried rather than lost.
In Spring Kafka, use DefaultErrorHandler with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer for declarative DLQ handling.
